processing: A tree-type, seed-propagated cultivar rather than one finished tea. Its leaf is regarded as suited to broken black tea, and the same leaf also goes into local green teas such as Shuiman.
harvest_season: Buds break early, in the first days of February, among the earliest flushes in China. No particular picking is documented as prized.
appearance_dry: As broken black tea, typically small dark reddish-brown particles; the leaf has little down.
appearance_liquor: As broken black tea, typically a deep, bright red-brown.
appearance_wet: Typical of large-leaf tea: broad, thick leaf pieces, coppery after oxidation.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about this cultivar's cup. Expect what is typical of large-leaf broken black tea: a strong, brisk, malty brew that takes milk well.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for broken black tea, brewed Western-style. Small particles extract fast, so shorten the steep if it turns harsh.

vintage_note: Not normally sold as a named tea with its own vintages; the cultivar reaches the buyer inside Hainan black and green teas. As is usual for those classes, buy the current or previous year and check the picking date. Very early spring picking is the region's selling point.
description:
Hainan Daye is a tea plant before it is a tea: a tall, tree-type cultivar native to Wuzhishan in the tropical middle of Hainan island, and recognised as a national-level improved cultivar in China. What sets it apart is the climate. It wakes up in early February, when most Chinese tea gardens are still asleep.

The plant grows high with sparse branches, sets little seed, carries little down on the leaf and handles cold poorly, which is why it stays in the tropical south. It is grown mainly in Baoting, Qiongzhong and Baisha, and it is regarded as a good base for broken black tea.

Little is written about how it tastes on its own. If you meet it as a broken black, treat it like other large-leaf black teas: short Western steeps, strong cup, milk welcome. Shuiman green tea from Wuzhishan uses wild plants of this type and is the way to try the same leaf in a very different style.

You are unlikely to see the cultivar name on a packet unless the seller is proud of it. Ask whether a Hainan tea uses local large-leaf plants or leaf from imported cultivars, because both grow on the island.
history:
The cultivar originates at Wuzhishan and later spread to Baoting, Qiongzhong and Baisha. In 1958 Baoting county founded the Hongqi tea farm at Tongshi, in what is now Wuzhishan city, and it worked mainly with wild plants of this type.

Compared with Sichuan large-leaf and the Yunnan Shuangjiang and Fengqing large-leaf types, it is described as having relatively high chromosomal variation. The date it was named a national improved cultivar is not well documented.
